paragraphs.heading: A great city of the Indus
paragraphs.text: Mohenjo-daro is an archaeological site in Pakistan, in the Larkana District of Sindh. The city was built around 2500 BCE by the Indus Valley Civilisation, which is also called the Harappan Civilisation. In its day it ranked among the biggest settlements of that civilisation, and it was one of the earliest major cities anywhere. Its contemporaries included ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Minoa and Norte Chico.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits and what it was called
paragraphs.text: The site lies off the west bank of the lower Indus river, on a ridge in the river's flood plain, around 28 kilometres from the town of Larkana. Nobody knows what its builders called it. The modern name has been read as “Mound of the Dead” in Sindhi. The scholar Iravatham Mahadevan studied a seal from the site and guessed that the old name might have meant “city of the cockerel”.

paragraphs.heading: A city built on a plan
paragraphs.text: Mohenjo-daro was laid out on a grid, with straight-sided buildings set in rows. Most were made of brick that had been fired and set with mortar, though some used sun-dried mud brick and timber upper parts. The city is thought to have covered 300 hectares, and one cautious estimate puts its peak population near 40,000. A place this large, with public buildings and shared facilities, points to a highly organised society. It was split into two parts, known as the Citadel and the Lower City.

paragraphs.heading: Wells, drains and courtyards
paragraphs.text: A large well stood in the central marketplace, while single households or groups of households drew water from smaller wells. Dirty water ran into covered drains along the main streets. Some houses, probably those of higher-status people, had rooms that seem to have been kept for bathing. One building even had an underground furnace, called a hypocaust, perhaps for heated baths. Most homes had an inner courtyard with doors onto side lanes, and some had two storeys.

paragraphs.heading: The Citadel and the Great Bath
paragraphs.text: The Citadel was a mound of mud brick about 12 metres high. It held public baths, a big residential building meant for about 5,000 citizens, and two large halls for gatherings. One large and elaborate public bath, often called the Great Bath, stands near a building known as the “Great Granary”. Steps lead down from a courtyard lined with columns into a brick pool, made watertight with a coat of bitumen. The pool is 12 metres long, 7 metres wide and 2.4 metres deep, and it may have been used for religious cleansing.

paragraphs.heading: Granary or great hall
paragraphs.text: Close to the Great Bath is a large building that Sir Mortimer Wheeler named the “Great Granary” in 1950. He took certain divisions in its heavy wooden upper structure to be bays for storing grain, with air channels to dry it. In his picture, carts carried grain in from the countryside and emptied it straight into the bays. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer has pointed out that no evidence of grain has been found there at all. He suggested calling it a “Great Hall” whose use is unknown.

paragraphs.heading: Decline and rediscovery
paragraphs.text: Mohenjo-daro thrived for several centuries. When the Indus civilisation fell into sudden decline around 1700 BCE, the city was left empty, as were its other large cities. The ruins were found again in the 1920s, and in 1980 the site became South Asia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. Digging stopped after 1965 because weather was damaging the exposed buildings, and since then only rescue digs, surveys and conservation work have been allowed. Drilling in 2015 showed the site is larger than the part uncovered, yet today it is threatened by erosion and poor restoration.
